transcript: In Hurt, Virginia a group of teenagers are recovering from loss, under the backdrop of a summer camp — Grief Camp, to be specific. This play takes place in a beautifully designed cabin, showcasing a collection of scenes that often don't explicitly make reference to the grief that’s simmering under the surface throughout the whole piece. I liked how understated it was, though some may find it a little unfocused or scattered. It's definitely more of a character study and a look at how these teenagers work through grief on a day to day basis. It's not so much about the dramatic catharsis that's often associated with loss, but the way that loss permeates our lives after we've experienced it. I enjoyed the performances and the writing, which I thought were really funny at times, and captured the awkwardness and philosophical expansiveness that show up in teenage interactions. And for the pace that this play moves at, 90 minutes was the perfect runtime, though part of me wishes we could have gotten a deeper dive into each of the characters and their backstories. Dramatically speaking, I can see some people critiquing the way that this play doesn't really go anywhere in that it spends way more time setting up different threads than it does closing or connecting them. But I think by the end, it has given you plenty to chew on and is very satisfying in that sense. Grief Camp is running at Atlantic through May 11th. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
